concepts.title: Ten Million Souls, No Place for Two
concepts.definition: Auden's blues opens on a city of ten million souls -- some in mansions, some in holes -- yet no place for the refugee couple. 'Says this city has ten million souls' refracts everything through the speaker's voice; passports and official papers have declared the two of them outside humanity's count.
concepts.key_idea: A city of millions with room for none -- statelessness as the denial of a species.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww119.txt opening stanzas (city has ten million souls, mansions and holes, no place for us, my dear, passport and official discrimination)

solution_steps.explain: Ten million souls can find rooms, yet the couple cannot -- abundance coexists with exclusion.
An expired or absent passport makes them legally invisible to committees and consuls.
Each stanza closes with 'my dear' -- private grief sung inside public catastrophe.

concepts.title: Nature's Generosity Against Human Doors
concepts.definition: Stanza by stanza, nature offers what society refuses: the old yew sprouting new leaves, the thrush singing its heart out, the fish swimming free, the birds in trees, doors opening for a cat and a dog. Against every natural welcome stands the human lock -- committees, consuls, soldiers, and the thunder of bombing planes.
concepts.key_idea: Even the fish are free -- Auden's catalogue shames every human door that stays shut.

solution_steps.explain: The yew renews itself, the thrush sings freely, fish and birds live unpoliced -- freedom is the norm of nature.
Committees offer talks, consuls tear up passes, soldiers bar the door -- bureaucracy and force close ranks.
Each natural generosity sharpens the cruelty of the man-made 'no'.

concepts.title: Blues Form and the Anonymity of Grief
concepts.definition: The poem borrows the blues form -- repeated first lines and a rueful refrain 'my dear' -- to give refugee grief the shape of a folk lament. The speakers remain unnamed: any refugee couple, any war, any city. The last stanza's looking through the blending snow to the sunless city and the thunder of planes leaves history's threat hanging.
concepts.key_idea: A folk-song shape for a modern disaster -- repetition, refrain and anonymity make grief universal.

solution_steps.explain: Each stanza repeats its opening line, then lands on the intimate refrain 'my dear' -- the blues pattern.
No names are given, so the couple stand for all the displaced of every war.
Snow blurs city and sky as bombing planes thunder -- the personal lament ends inside history's menace.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the contrast between the fish swimming free and the couple who cannot swim the river of bureaucracy.

solution_template.explain: The fish glide past ships without papers or permission -- nature demands no documents.
The refugees, with no valid papers, are turned away from even the meanest shelter.
Auden's irony: in a human world, freedom requires a stamp; nature grants what states withhold.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How does the blues form intensify the sorrow of the poem rather than lighten it?

solution_template.explain: Repeating the first line of each stanza forces the reader to hear the loss twice.
'My dear' turns each public wrong into a private tenderness between the couple.
The musical repetition becomes a tolling -- the form deepens grief instead of easing it.
